title: 464. Sets, Logic, Reasoning & Proof: Set Membership
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a number is an element of a listed set.
questions.question: Let \(A=\{1,3,5\}\). Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: The symbol \(\in\) means "is an element of". The number \(3\) appears in the list of elements of \(A\), so \(3\in A\). The number \(4\) does not appear in the list, so \(4\notin A\).
questions.hint: Check whether the number appears among the listed elements.

questions.question: What does the statement \(x\notin A\) mean?

options.label: A
options.text: \(x\) is not an element of the set \(A\).

questions.explanation: The symbol \(\notin\) is the negation of \(\in\). So \(x\notin A\) says that the object \(x\) is not one of the elements of \(A\). It makes a claim about an object and a set, not about one set being contained in another.
questions.hint: The symbol is the membership symbol with a stroke through it.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an element that is a set from the numbers inside it.
questions.question: Let \(A=\{1,\{2\},3\}\). Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: The three elements of \(A\) are the number \(1\), the set \(\{2\}\), and the number \(3\). So \(\{2\}\in A\). The number \(2\) itself is not listed as an element; it is an element of the element \(\{2\}\), which is a different statement.
questions.hint: List the elements of \(A\) exactly as they are written between the outer braces.

questions.concept: Membership in a set given by an equation
questions.learningObjective: Test membership in a set defined by an equation.
questions.question: Let \(A=\{x\in\mathbb{Z}\mid x^2=9\}\). Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: An integer belongs to \(A\) exactly when its square is \(9\). Since \((-3)^2=9\), \(-3\in A\). For \(9\) the square is \(81\), so \(9\notin A\); the number \(9\) is the value of \(x^2\), not a value of \(x\).
questions.hint: Substitute each candidate for \(x\) in the defining condition.

questions.learningObjective: Decide which non-membership statement is true.
questions.question: Let \(B=\{2,4,6,8\}\). Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: The number \(5\) does not appear among the elements \(2,4,6,8\), so \(5\notin B\) is true. The number \(6\) does appear, so \(6\in B\) and the statement \(6\notin B\) is false.
questions.hint: A non-membership statement is true exactly when the object is missing from the list.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a number from the set containing that number.
questions.question: Let \(A=\{1,2,3\}\). Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: The elements of \(A\) are the numbers \(1\), \(2\), and \(3\), so \(1\in A\). The set \(\{1\}\) is not one of these three numbers, so \(\{1\}\notin A\). It is true that \(\{1\}\subseteq A\), but that is a subset statement, not a membership statement.
questions.hint: Membership asks whether the object itself is listed; compare with what the subset symbol would say.

questions.concept: The empty set as an element
questions.learningObjective: Recognise that a set containing the empty set is not empty.
questions.question: Let \(A=\{\varnothing\}\). Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: The set \(A\) has exactly one element, and that element is the empty set. Therefore \(\varnothing\in A\). The set \(A\) is not empty: a box containing an empty box is not an empty box.
questions.hint: Count the objects written between the braces of \(A\).

questions.learningObjective: Test membership in a set defined by two conditions.
questions.question: Let \(C=\{n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid n>0,\ n\text{ is a multiple of }3,\ n<20\}\). Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: The number \(18\) is positive, is a multiple of \(3\) (\(18=3\cdot 6\)), and is less than \(20\), so \(18\in C\). The number \(21\) is a multiple of \(3\), but it is not less than \(20\), so it fails one condition and \(21\notin C\).
questions.hint: An element must satisfy every condition in the description, not just one of them.

questions.learningObjective: Read membership correctly in a set whose elements are themselves sets.
questions.question: Let \(A=\{1,\{1\},\{1,\{1\}\}\}\). Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: The three elements of \(A\) are \(1\), \(\{1\}\), and \(\{1,\{1\}\}\). So \(\{1,\{1\}\}\in A\). The set \(\{\{1\}\}\) has the single element \(\{1\}\); it is a subset of \(A\), but it is not one of the three listed elements.
questions.hint: Separate the top-level elements of \(A\) at the commas that are not inside inner braces.

questions.learningObjective: Decide membership of a number in standard number sets.
questions.question: Here \(\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\) denotes the positive integers. Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: The integers \(\mathbb{Z}\) include the negative whole numbers, so \(-5\in\mathbb{Z}\). The set \(\mathbb{N}\) as defined here contains only positive integers, so \(-5\notin\mathbb{N}\). The second statement reverses the two sets.
questions.hint: Recall which of the two number sets contains negative whole numbers.
